spec.title: The before picture, machine-checked
spec.intro:
This is the mindset lab — no terminal, no tooling, just the one intellectual move the
whole program exists to make routine. You will write the one-page legacy-vs-engineered
analysis of a real control you own, in the exact fixed shape the capstone re-opens at
the end of the program. Three files are in your workspace: a conforming exemplar (the
laptop-encryption worked example from §5.1 — the claim thread you will meet again in
almost every module), a legacy-only counterexample, and your own template. The "Run
validator" button runs the module's own structural rubric check — the same logic this
curriculum's CI runs against its own lab — and its verdict is earned, not scripted:
it really rejects, then really accepts, whatever your document currently says. One
honesty note: the check is structural. Passing it is the floor, not the grade — the
honest sentences are yours to write.

tasks.instruction:
Before writing a word: read the exemplar (`lab00/legacy-vs-engineered-laptop-encryption.md`)
to calibrate, then press **Run validator** with your template untouched. Watch the
check reject it — naming every missing legacy problem, every missing loop stage,
and the missing inversion statement. A check that cannot reject is not a check;
this is the same discrimination assertion the module's CI makes against its own lab.

verify.stdout_matches: missing legacy problem: manual toil[\s\S]*missing loop stage: OWN[\s\S]*missing reality->policy inversion statement

hints.nudge: Don't write anything yet. Run the check against the empty template and read every line it emits — that list is your work plan.

hints.concept: §4.1 — a control is a falsifiable claim; a rubric that can't fail a bad document verifies nothing

hints.reveal: Press Run validator with the template as-is. It exits 1 and lists 13 gaps: 5 problems, 7 stages, 1 inversion statement.

tasks.explain:
You just watched evidence-grade verification do its first job: discriminate. The
thirteen lines it printed are the exact contract your document must satisfy — and
because the check evaluates your real current text, the pass you earn later is a
genuine state change, not a quiz answer.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 1 — name the control as a claim. In your template's **Control as a claim**
section, pick one real control your organization owns (one you privately suspect is
run the legacy way) and write it as a single falsifiable sentence: "X is true of
system Y." If you can't phrase it that way, you picked a policy — pick again. Then
add a line stating where the truth of that claim physically lives today, in the
form "Truth lives today in: …" — name the actual config file, API, log, DB row, or
cloud setting.

hints.nudge: Strip the policy language until reality can make the sentence true or false. "Access reviews are performed quarterly" is a process; "no disabled employee has an active account" is a claim.

hints.concept: §4.1 — a control is a claim about system state

hints.reveal: Under the first heading write e.g.: 'Claim: MFA is required for every production-console login.' and 'Truth lives today in: the identity provider's authentication policy API and its sign-in event log.'

tasks.explain:
The moment a control reads "X is true of system Y," you can ask system Y whether X
holds — which is the whole job. Naming where the truth physically lives is LOCATE
before you've met the loop: every later module starts exactly here.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 2 — score your control against all five legacy problems (§4.3), one honest
sentence each, in the **Five-problem scorecard** section. All five must be named by
name: manual toil, transactional relationship, whack-a-mole, closed-framework
focus, commoditized compliance. "N/A" is allowed only with a one-line justification.

hints.nudge: One sentence per problem, each problem named exactly (hyphens matter: whack-a-mole, closed-framework). The exemplar's scorecard shows the shape.

hints.concept: §4.3 — the five problems with legacy GRC

hints.reveal: Five lines, e.g.: '- Manual toil, trivial output: …' '- Transactional relationship: …' '- Whack-a-mole: …' '- Closed-framework focus: …' '- Commoditized compliance: …' — each finished with an honest sentence about YOUR control.

tasks.explain:
Naming all five forces the uncomfortable audit: most controls fail several at once,
and the trap problem — commoditized compliance — is the one a tooling enthusiast
walks into first. If a future "improvement" only makes the toil cheaper, you now
have the sentence on file that says so.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 3 — map the legacy arrow. In the **Legacy arrow** section, describe in one
or two sentences how this control is verified today, writing the chain out as
framework -> controls -> implementation -> evidence -> audit on one line, and note
specifically where reality is consulted (usually: last, by hand, periodically).
The module's own CI does not check this section — the in-app check here is
deliberately stricter, because the capstone diffs against it.

hints.nudge: Write the five-stage chain with arrows on a single line, then answer: at which arrow does anyone actually look at the running system — and how often?

hints.concept: §4.2 — the inversion thesis: which end of the arrow you start from

hints.reveal: e.g. 'Today this control runs framework -> controls -> implementation -> evidence -> audit: reality is consulted last, by hand, once a quarter.'

tasks.explain:
Writing the arrow down makes the diagnosis structural instead of personal: nobody
on the legacy path is lazy — the *direction* guarantees reality is consulted last.
That sentence is the "before" the capstone will hold your engineered control against.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 4 — map the engineered arrow. In the **Engineered arrow** section, walk the
SAME control through all seven loop stages, one line each, in loop order, using the
uppercase stage tokens: UNDERSTAND, LOCATE, QUERY, EVALUATE, EVIDENCE, MONITOR, OWN
(the tokens are the contract — the rubric matches them case-sensitively). Each line
is "STAGE: detail". Be concrete at LOCATE — name the actual system that holds the
truth.

hints.nudge: Seven lines, loop order, UPPERCASE tokens followed by a colon. The §3 worked pair: LOCATE is the MDM's device API, QUERY is the authenticated call, EVALUATE is 'flag == on for every device'.

hints.reveal: e.g. '- UNDERSTAND: the claim is …' '- LOCATE: the truth lives in <the named system>.' '- QUERY: …' '- EVALUATE: …' '- EVIDENCE: …' '- MONITOR: …' '- OWN: …'

tasks.explain:
That seven-line map is the table of contents for your entire program: each line
becomes a module, and the file you just wrote it in becomes the capstone's input.
The uppercase tokens aren't pedantry — they're the machine-readable spine the
module-15 validator (and this one) keys on.

tasks.instruction:
§6 task 5 — state the inversion in your own words. Close the **Inversion statement**
section with one sentence contrasting the two arrows for THIS control: what changes
when reality drives the policy instead of the document. Make the direction explicit —
"reality -> policy", or say it: reality drives the policy.

hints.nudge: One sentence, this control, both arrows. The §3 closer is the shape: legacy asks the document whether reality complied; engineering asks reality and rewrites the document to match.

hints.reveal: e.g. 'Reality -> policy: instead of asking the binder whether the fleet complied, we ask the fleet continuously and let what it reports drive the policy and the proof.'

tasks.explain:
If you internalize one sentence from module 00, it's the one you just wrote. Every
technique in the next fifteen modules is instrumentation for that arrow — and you
phrased it for a control you actually own, which is what makes it commit you.

tasks.instruction:
The deliverable. Press **Run validator** again: your analysis must now PASS the
same check that rejected the empty template in step 1 — exit 0, no missing lines.
That fail-then-pass pair is your first piece of engineered evidence, and the
document itself is the *before* half of the program-long before/after: module 15
re-opens this exact artifact. On your own machine you'd save it as
legacy-vs-engineered-<control>.md and keep it.

hints.nudge: If it still exits 1, the output names each gap exactly — fix only what it names. Lowercase stage tokens and missing hyphens are the classic near-misses.

hints.concept: §6 deliverables — the fixed shape exists so the capstone can diff against it

hints.reveal: Complete all five sections per t2–t6 (the exemplar shows a full conforming document), then press Run validator: it prints nothing and exits 0.

tasks.explain:
The verdict you just earned is re-runnable: anyone with your document and this
check gets the same answer, which is what separates evidence from assertion. Keep
the artifact — the capstone diffs your fully-engineered control against this exact
before picture, and the delta is the proof the program worked.

tasks.instruction:
The defense, in writing (4–6 sentences): state the inversion thesis cold — no notes,
no peeking at §3 — then pick ONE of the five principles (§4.4) and connect it to the
specific legacy problem it answers, using your control as the example. This is the
spoken-defense half of the module's assessment, rehearsed.

hints.nudge: The thesis is one sentence about direction, not technology. Then: name a principle, name its problem — if you can't pair them, you've memorized a slogan, not the model.

hints.concept: §4.4 — the five principles, each a response to a named problem

files.content:
# Legacy-vs-Engineered Analysis: Laptop Encryption

## Control as a claim
Claim: Every employee laptop has full-disk encryption enabled.
Truth lives today in: the MDM device API (per-device encryption status), reachable right now.

## Five-problem scorecard (legacy)
- Manual toil, trivial output: an analyst collects a handful of encryption screenshots each quarter.
- Transactional relationship: IT is chased for evidence near audit time, treated as an evidence source.
- Whack-a-mole: a single drifted laptop is fixed once it is noticed, not the enrollment gap that caused it.
- Closed-framework focus: effort optimizes the SOC 2 binder wording rather than actual fleet encryption.
- Commoditized compliance: prior "automation" just emailed one screenshot faster, adding no assurance.

## Legacy arrow
Verified today as framework -> controls -> implementation -> evidence -> audit: reality is consulted
LAST, by hand, once a quarter, on a small sample.

## Engineered arrow (seven-stage loop)
- UNDERSTAND: the claim is "every laptop is encrypted, right now."
- LOCATE: the truth lives in the MDM device API.
- QUERY: authenticated, fully paginated call listing every enrolled device.
- EVALUATE: encryption flag == on for every device, expressed as policy-as-code.
- EVIDENCE: the full API response plus the pass/fail verdict, written to a versioned store.
- MONITOR: re-run on a schedule; alert the owner when any device flips to non-compliant.
- OWN: a named owner, with time-to-remediate-drift as the product metric.

## Inversion statement
Reality -> policy: instead of asking the binder whether the fleet complied, we ask the fleet
continuously and let what it reports drive the policy and the proof.
